Hey Voat, I'm really loving the community here so I thought you guys would like to hear the story of the new album I recently released. Get ready for a tl;dr.

First of all, you can listen to the album here and theres a free download link in the description: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aI5MWIgN9Lo

As a brief overview of the album, it was inspired by the guitar licks of Slash, the style and lyrics of Pink Floyd, and the composition of classical composers (Ill explain that later). I wrote and recorded the entire album in my college dorm room, playing guitar, piano, and bass myself, sending the drums to my friend in ohio, and a classmate of mine for vocals.

As for the composition, heres where things got interesting. Classical composers use a technique where they take reference melodies from well known pieces and work them in to an entirely new piece. Often times these melodies were so well hidden in the piece, an untrained ear would never detect them. For each song in my album, I wanted to incorporate this technique. Every song has a reference melody that is intended to add to the message of the piece. If I havent lost you guys yet, Ill describe each melody used now.

1) The River

The melody of Westminister Quarters is used all around the world in churches and clocks to mark the time of day. Here, the melody creates a chord progression for the guitar, which is imitated by the piano one measure behind. It is followed by a saxophone solo with a beating drum and bassline. The melody is believed to have been inspired by Handel’s Messiah “I know that my Redeemer Liveth.” It was composed in 1793 by Dr. Joseph Jowett and Dr. John Randall for the clock at the Cambridge University Church’s clock. There is some speculation, however, that the melody was also composed by Dr. Randall’s student, William Crotch. In the mid 1800’s, the melody was adopted by Westminister Palace and became a traditional tune for clocks.

2) The Act

Gregorian Plainchant, Dies Irae, is an early chant from the Catholic Church. Believed to be written by either Thomas of Celano or Latino Malabranca Orsini, first accounts of the chant are from the 13th century, however the chant itself may be much older as records from that time are poor. Translated, the text means “Day of Wrath” and is often played at Catholic funerals. The melody is frequently referenced by other composers, including Mozart, who utilized both the melody and lyrics in a piece of his own with the same name, and the intro music to the movie “The Shining.” Here, the melody can be found both in the bassline and the piano. The melody is taken as is from the chant for the bass, while creating a chord progression that the piano follows. The vocals also follow the original chant while the guitar outlines a riff loosely based on the key of the chant.

3) Breathe (my personal favorite)

“All is Lost”, a movie featuring Robert Redford, follows the journey of a man lost at sea. While the movie itself features no dialog, Alexander Ebert’s compositions fill in the almost silent movie. His composition, “Excelsior”, serves as the main theme throughout the movie, featuring a hauntingly beautiful flute solo. His work, along with the story itself, captures the feelings of loneliness and solitude perfectly as it follows a man who may well be on his way to death after his ship becomes lost at sea. The melody of the flute solo was taken to create the bassline for this track as well as laying the progression for the chords of the piano. The lyrics also use the same melody at a different rate and with some slight variation.

4) The Grand Finale

Gloria in excelsis Deo, an old Catholic hymn, was traditionally used in masses as a praise of God (a section of mass known as the Gloria). According to the Bible, the lyrics of the original hymn were the words sung by the angels who announced Christ’s birth to the shepherds. In this piece, the melody again creates the bassline from which the other instruments build upon. Though the original composer remains unknown, the hymn gained recognition in the second and third centuries from composers who would use the melody in their own works. At this time period, it was traditional to use melodies from hymns and chants in new music. The composition of entirely new melodies was, in fact, rare, as Composers instead would take melodies from previous pieces and turn them into something new.

5) Curtain Call

The Silence of the Lambs follows the story of Dr. Hannibal Lecter, a psychiatrist with a taste for human flesh locked in a mental hospital in Baltimore. The soundtrack for the film was composed by Howard Shore, a well known composer most famous for his work on the Lord of the Rings soundtrack. The Silence of the Lambs contains a piece entitled “Clarice”, a beautiful yet somewhat eerie melody that captures the story of one killer hunting another through a green FBI agent. Here, the main melody of the piece is taken as the bassline. Piano and guitar is added over that with vocals that somewhat mimic the guitar. After the lyrics, the song turns into a loose jam over the “Clarice” melody. The melody is often heard when the protagonist, Clarice Starling, meets the cannibalistic mad-man, Hannibal Lecter, a man synonymous with death.

Well guys, thank you for reading. I know this was a long one, but I put a lot of work into this album and there was no other way for me to share all the passion I have put into it. I hope you can appreciate the amount of work I've put into making this album, and I hope youll give it a listen. All that matters to me at the end of the day is that someone hears what I've written. Thanks again guys!

-Eric O'Neill
